newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: TELECOM NOT BULLET PROOF AGAINST NZ ECONOMY.
newsitem.headline: TELECOM NOT BULLET PROOF AGAINST NZ ECONOMY.

text.p: New Zealand's bellwether stock, Telecom Corp of New Zealand, is expected to produce flat first quarter earnings when it reports on Tuesday.
Analysts on Thursday said the result would be within NZ$5 million of $190 million, against the 1996 June quarter's $177.1 million, which included abnormal losses from Pacific Star.
The focus of the result will be how much the slower-than- expected economic growth in New Zealand had hurt Telecom and to what extent cost-cutting initiatives were coming through.

"On the cost side, it is probably a little bit early at this stage for everything they are doing, or intending to do, to have impacted strongly. Most benefits will occur later in the year," said Merrill Lynch analyst Michelle Eisig.
"On the revenue side the company has indicated that the first couple of months of the quarter were relatively strong, all things considered," she said.
"The key driver of reveue growth is likely to have continued to have been enhanced network services."
Telecom Chief Executive Roderick Deane said a month ago at the company's annual meeting that Telecom performed satisfactorily in the first quarter given the slow economy.
Like all New Zealand companies, he said Telecom, owned a quarter each by Bell Atlantic and Ameritech, was having difficulty growing earnings.
Deane also expressed confidence that Telecom would capture additional cost savings via its Performance 2000 programme.
An analyst who declined to be named said economic conditions were awful. He forecast a $187 million profit and an annual profit of $800 million, up from $770 million (before abnormals).

"They are a broadly-based company dealing with everyone in New Zealand, businesses are finding it tough so everything is being scaled back a little bit. Telecom is not bullet proof to the general state of the economy."
ANZ Securities senior analyst Andrew Butterell said there was some scepticism in the market whether Deane could squeeze out further cost savings but he was not in that camp.
"You will start seeing it in this quarter but the full effects will come through later in the year," he said.
He expects to see a revival in the growth rate of cellular business which started to flag comparatively last quarter.
"I think there is a lot of growth that can come out of the New Zealand cellular market because of the competition that Bell South has instigated at long last," he said.
Cellular costs are expected to fall further and that will provide Telecom with further growth.

Telecom had a startling performance in its share price during the quarter ended June, thanks mainly to a big rally in domestic bonds and an equally big rally in equities in the markets of English-speaking nations.

Share manager at National Mutual Funds Management, John Norling, said Telecom's price, which rose from $6.27 on March 14 to over $8.00 on July 29, also gained as sentiment on the stock improved, and in response to buying from foreign institutions.
News at the last quarter result that Telecom had cleaned up its Pacific Star mess in Australia and was taking action on costs had lifted market confidence.
National Mutual has gone from overweight to underweight but Telecom's fall to $7.40 was tempting Norling again, he added.

Butterell considered Telecom at fair value but said it was likely to continue to outperform other telco firms over the long term because it takes a long-term view on issues such as the internet, cable and broadband services.

A possible downside for Telecom ahead could be the listing in November of Telstra, with some foreign investors switching out of Telecom in favour of the Australian giant -- likely to be the biggest IPO in the world in 1997.

"It's possible it may promote switching out of what is seen as quite a mature telco to one that is at a much earlier stage of its development and certainly has more fat to come out of it," said one analyst.
